name: Polyurethane-coated breast implants

card.summary: Silicone breast implants covered in a thin polyurethane foam layer, used in breast augmentation and reconstruction to keep a rounder, softer, stable-looking breast shape by lowering the chance of capsular contracture.
card.aka: polyurethane implants, foam-covered implants, PU implants
card.note: Not approved by the FDA for sale in the US; the foam can break down into a compound studied for carcinogenicity in animals, and removal can be harder.

quick.overview:
Polyurethane-coated breast implants are silicone gel implants wrapped in a micro-thin layer of polyurethane foam. They are used for cosmetic breast augmentation, revision surgery and reconstruction. The look people are after is a natural, soft, well-positioned breast that stays that way over the years.

The foam surface tends to bond with surrounding tissue, which surgeons say keeps the implant from rotating and reduces capsular contracture, the tightening scar capsule that can make a breast firm and distorted. A 2016 systematic review reported contracture rates of roughly 0.4-1% at six years for polyurethane-coated implants in augmentation, compared with 2-15% for textured silicone, while noting that the polyurethane studies were limited.[1]
quick.how: A plastic surgeon places the implant through an incision, typically in the crease under the breast or another approach, in a pocket under the muscle or breast tissue. Surgeons who use them describe a learning curve, because the sticky foam surface needs a precisely sized pocket and careful handling.[2] They are mostly available in Europe, Brazil and parts of South America and Asia rather than the US.
quick.risks: Risks include those of any breast implant: infection, contracture, asymmetry, rupture and reoperation. Specific to this type, the foam can degrade into 2,4-toluenediamine (TDA), which caused cancers in animal studies; the FDA concluded the resulting risk was negligible.[5] Foam-covered implants can be harder to remove, and polyurethane and textured implants have both been associated with breast implant-associated anaplastic large-cell lymphoma (BIA-ALCL), a rare lymphoma.[5]

lead: Polyurethane-coated breast implants are silicone gel breast implants whose shell is covered by a thin layer of polyurethane foam. They are used in cosmetic breast augmentation, in revision surgery after problems with earlier implants, and in breast reconstruction.[1][2]

For looks, the appeal is a stable, natural-looking result. Foam-covered implants are described by their surgeons as integrating with surrounding tissue, which helps hold the implant in position and lowers the rate of capsular contracture, the hardening of scar tissue around an implant that can make a breast tight, round and misshapen.[1][3]

Published studies, mostly surgeon case series and a systematic review, report low contracture rates. Concerns documented in the literature include difficult removal, a learning curve for surgeons, and the breakdown of the foam into 2,4-toluenediamine (TDA), which led to a period of reduced use and to the implants never being approved in the US.[5][2]

angle.text: Breast augmentation with a polyurethane-coated implant adds volume and shape at the time of surgery. Surgeons who use the coating say it helps the result stay soft and well positioned over time by limiting contracture and rotation.

paras: The implant is a silicone gel-filled device with a shell covered by a layer of polyurethane foam. The coating is intended to provoke a particular tissue reaction at the surface: histological studies describe a thin, vascular capsule with disorganised collagen rather than the dense, aligned capsule seen around many smooth implants.[3] Newer products use a micro-thin foam layer, and surgeons have studied them in both cosmetic and reconstructive settings, including prepectoral reconstruction.[4]

Polyurethane-covered implants were among the second-generation breast implants of the 1970s, introduced to reduce capsular contracture.[5] The coating can degrade in the body into 2,4-toluenediamine, a by-product that caused liver and skin cancers in animal studies, which prompted a brief halt in medical use of the implants. The FDA concluded the resulting cancer risk was negligible, and no manufacturer has sought US approval for the implants; they remain in use in Europe and South America.[5]

Interest returned from the 2010s, when surgeons published long-term series. One surgeon reported 30 years of experience with 382 aesthetic augmentation patients.[6] Another reported 525 patients with high satisfaction and a low incidence of capsular contracture, implant rotation and late seroma.[7] A 2015 review of 41 papers concluded there was no evidence of polyurethane-related cancer in studies longer than five years.[3]

Patients choose polyurethane-coated implants mainly for a natural result that persists. In revision surgery after contracture, surgeons use them in an attempt to prevent recurrence; a prospective five-year study of polyurethane implants in revisional augmentation was published in 2024.[8] In reconstruction after mastectomy, a retrospective study compared polyurethane with textured implants with a focus on contracture.[9]

Surgeons who use the implants describe their own technique issues. A systematic review of errors with polyurethane implants grouped them into planning errors, pocket-development errors and surface-dependent errors related to the foam, and described a learning curve.[2]

General implant risks apply: infection, asymmetry, malposition, rupture and reoperation. Specific to polyurethane implants, a review noted that they may be difficult to remove.[3] A paper on removal technique discusses the extra effort involved.[10] The foam's TDA degradation product and the lack of US approval remain the main regulatory points.[5]

Breast implant-associated anaplastic large-cell lymphoma (BIA-ALCL) is a rare lymphoma linked to textured and polyurethane-covered implants. Researchers have linked chronic bacterial biofilm and T-cell infiltration to implant surfaces in capsules and animal models.[11] The WHO recognised BIA-ALCL in 2016, and US lifetime risk estimates range widely, from 1 in 70,000 to 1 in 500,000 women with implants.[5]

A 2016 systematic review of 18 studies compared polyurethane-coated with textured silicone implants. It reported capsular contracture rates of 1.8-3.4% for polyurethane in primary reconstruction versus 10-15% for silicone at six years, and 0.4-1% versus 2-15% in primary augmentation, while noting the polyurethane studies had limitations and revision data were unclear.[1]

The 30-year follow-up of 382 augmentation patients examined contracture with the longest observation to date.[6] A 2015 review of 41 papers found a well-defined foreign-body capsule with low contracture and no evidence of cancer after five years.[3] Registered studies include a completed 237-patient data collection of prepectoral reconstruction with polyurethane implants and a 632-patient adverse event and satisfaction study of Silimed implants.[12][13] A 2026 narrative review of capsular contracture lists polyurethane coating among the surface factors under study.[14]

timeline.event: Polyurethane-covered implants introduced among second-generation implants to reduce capsular contracture.[5]
MD Anderson researchers establish the link between BIA-ALCL and implants (study of 60 women).[5]
A 30-year follow-up of polyurethane-coated implants in 382 augmentation patients is published.[6]
WHO recognises BIA-ALCL; a systematic review compares polyurethane with textured silicone.[1][5]
Prospective five-year study of polyurethane implants in revisional augmentation published.[8]
